classification.difficultyReason: Identify the base and exponent directly, recognising an unwritten exponent of 1.

questions.mappingNote: Every part assesses naming the base and index, including implicit index 1 and explicit index 0; evaluating the powers is not requested.
questions.methodNote: Identify the base and the superscript index using the definitions on page 2. Use b^1=b for an unwritten index; page 6 supplies the zero-power context.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the base and exponent directly, recognising an unwritten exponent of 1.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the repeated prime factor and count its occurrences in each small whole number.

questions.mappingNote: Each of parts a–f asks for exactly this conversion. Prime factorisation is the directly assessed skill; identifying the exponent supports the notation.
questions.methodNote: Page 2, Example 2 expands a number into repeated identical prime factors, then counts those factors to write a prime-base power. The index-notation definition explains the factor count.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the repeated prime factor and count its occurrences in each small whole number.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate positive whole-number powers and multiply the resulting numerical values.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly assess numerical evaluation of index notation; parts e and f also require multiplication of the evaluated powers.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 defines a positive integer power as repeated multiplication of equal factors. Evaluate each power before multiplying separate powers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate positive whole-number powers and multiply the resulting numerical values.

classification.difficultyReason: Decompose whole numbers into prime factors and collect repeated factors using indices.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly assess expressing a whole number as a product of prime powers; prime-factorisation is the closest catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Prime decomposition followed by collecting repeated prime factors in index notation, as in Examples 2 and 3. Example 3 also uses a preliminary composite-factor decomposition.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Decompose whole numbers into prime factors and collect repeated factors using indices.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the same-base multiplication law directly, multiplying numerical coefficients where present.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–f apply numerical same-base multiplication; g–l extend the same method to algebraic terms, with coefficient multiplication in i–l. The most advanced directly assessed skill is applying index laws to algebraic terms.
questions.methodNote: Index law 1 adds indices when multiplying powers of the same base. Example 4 applies this to numerical powers, variables and coefficients; an unprinted index is 1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the same-base multiplication law directly, multiplying numerical coefficients where present.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct multiplication of algebraic terms using coefficient multiplication and addition of positive indices.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly apply the algebraic multiplication method in Example 4c–d; no fraction operations or powers of products are required.
questions.methodNote: Index law 1 adds indices when multiplying powers of the same base. Example 4 combines numerical coefficients and adds indices separately for each variable.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct multiplication of algebraic terms using coefficient multiplication and addition of positive indices.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the quotient law directly, recognise implied indices of one, and divide numerical coefficients in the algebraic fractions.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–f apply the quotient law to numerical bases; g–h apply it to a variable; i–l simplify algebraic fractions by dividing coefficients and subtracting indices.
questions.methodNote: Index law 2 subtracts indices when dividing powers with the same base. Example 5 separates numerical coefficients from powers and treats an unprinted index as one.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the quotient law directly, recognise implied indices of one, and divide numerical coefficients in the algebraic fractions.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the zero-index rule directly to individual factors.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly applies the zero index to algebraic factors; coefficients and factors without a zero index remain.
questions.methodNote: Use the stated rule that a non-zero base raised to zero equals 1, then multiply the remaining factors, as demonstrated in Example 8.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the zero-index rule directly to individual factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Directly divide coefficients and subtract indices for each variable; no reframing or choice of an unfamiliar method is required.

questions.mappingNote: Every part is an algebraic quotient with positive integer indices; parts e–h also require coefficient division. The assessed skill is simplifying algebraic fractions involving indices.
questions.methodNote: Index law 2 subtracts indices when dividing powers with the same base. Example 5 separates numerical coefficients from variable powers before simplifying; Example 6 continues coefficient and index simplification.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Directly divide coefficients and subtract indices for each variable; no reframing or choice of an unfamiliar method is required.

classification.difficultyReason: Multiply and divide algebraic fractions, combining coefficients and indices of two variables.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts directly practise Example 6; parts a–d multiply algebraic fractions and e–h divide them. The other supplied reuse candidates have different complete tasks and are ineligible.
questions.methodNote: Example 6 multiplies numerators and denominators, then simplifies coefficients and subtracts indices. Division is first rewritten as multiplication by the reciprocal.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Multiply and divide algebraic fractions, combining coefficients and indices of two variables.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer missing algebraic factors and divisors by reversing multiplication and division index laws.

questions.mappingNote: Each missing factor is the printed product divided by its known factor; each missing divisor is the printed dividend divided by its quotient. This reverses the taught product and quotient calculations.
questions.methodNote: Index laws 1 and 2 and Examples 4–6 combine or subtract indices for matching bases and calculate coefficients separately.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Infer missing algebraic factors and divisors by reversing multiplication and division index laws.

classification.difficultyReason: Simplifies algebraic quotients using index laws and verifies three results by substitution, including a negative value.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts assess simplification of algebraic fractions involving indices. Parts a–c additionally require substitution checks; the supplied teaching pages do not demonstrate substitution, including substitution of negative values.
questions.methodNote: Apply the quotient law by subtracting indices and dividing numerical coefficients, as in Example 5e–f. Page 5 establishes the zero-index rule needed in part g.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Simplifies algebraic quotients using index laws and verifies three results by substitution, including a negative value.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the base of each zero power, distinguish external coefficients from bracketed bases, and perform the remaining simple arithmetic.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve parts directly assess algebraic zero indices, including sums, differences and bracketed expressions. The printed Example 9 margin reference is retained in the prompt.
questions.methodNote: Use the stated rule that a non-zero base raised to zero is 1. Example 9 distinguishes a complete bracketed base from a coefficient outside a power; substitute 1 for zero powers and complete the arithmetic.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the base of each zero power, distinguish external coefficients from bracketed bases, and perform the remaining simple arithmetic.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct application of the power-of-a-power law to numerical and algebraic bases.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess multiplying inner and outer positive-integer indices; the algebraic parts determine the primary skill.
questions.methodNote: Index law 3 on page 3 states that raising a power to a power multiplies the indices: $(a^m)^n=a^{mn}$. Pages 5–6 demonstrate applying index laws to bracketed powers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct application of the power-of-a-power law to numerical and algebraic bases.

classification.difficultyReason: Combines powers of powers with multiplication and division, progressing to multi-factor algebraic fractions.

questions.mappingNote: Question 15 directly combines the laws on page 3 with the algebraic-fraction operations and bracket expansions illustrated on page 5 and product powers on page 6. The final parts most directly assess algebraic fractions involving indices.
questions.methodNote: Use the power-of-a-power law before combining like bases. For fractions, multiply numerators and denominators; change division to multiplication by the reciprocal. Raise every factor of a product to its power.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines powers of powers with multiplication and division, progressing to multi-factor algebraic fractions.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the explicitly named power-of-a-power law to recover missing indices or base powers by division; for the final completion, choose two positive integer indices whose product is 20.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly applies the positive-integer power-of-a-power law. Part i intentionally permits multiple completions.
questions.methodNote: Index law 3 states that raising a power to a power multiplies the indices: $(a^m)^n=a^{mn}$. Complete each missing index or base power by matching that product.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use the explicitly named power-of-a-power law to recover missing indices or base powers by division; for the final completion, choose two positive integer indices whose product is 20.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare two applications of the power-of-a-power law and generalise using commutativity of multiplication.

questions.mappingNote: Question 17 directly explores the power-of-a-power law and asks for a general statement, so establishing index laws is the primary skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 3, index law 3, gives $(a^m)^n=a^{mn}$; pages 5–6 show applying powers to algebraic expressions. Compare both sides by multiplying indices, then generalise using $mn=nm$.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare two applications of the power-of-a-power law and generalise using commutativity of multiplication.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply powers to every factor or fraction component, including coefficients and existing powers.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d raise products to powers; e–h raise quotients to powers. Parts c, d and h additionally use the power-of-a-power law. The printed Example 7 cross-reference is retained.
questions.methodNote: Index laws 3–5 distribute a power across a product or quotient and multiply nested indices. Example 7 expands powers of fractions component by component; Example 9 applies the same method to algebraic products.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply powers to every factor or fraction component, including coefficients and existing powers.

classification.difficultyReason: Combines powers of products with multiplication of algebraic terms; the final two parts also use the zero index.

questions.mappingNote: Page 3 supplies index laws 1, 3 and 4. Example 7 on page 5 models expanding powered brackets. Example 9 on page 6 directly models powered algebraic products and a zero-power factor multiplied by another powered term.
questions.methodNote: Raise every factor in a product to the outer power, multiply indices for a power of a power, and add indices when multiplying equal bases. Apply the zero-index rule in parts e and f.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines powers of products with multiplication of algebraic terms; the final two parts also use the zero index.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand powers of algebraic fractions, then multiply or divide and simplify using index laws.

questions.mappingNote: Page 3 states the relevant index laws. Page 5 Example 7c–d demonstrates expanding powered fractions and reciprocal multiplication. Page 6 provides further algebraic index-law simplification. Question 20 combines these methods.
questions.methodNote: Apply the power-of-a-power and power-of-a-quotient laws; expand each bracket, replace division by multiplication by the reciprocal, and simplify coefficients and like-base powers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand powers of algebraic fractions, then multiply or divide and simplify using index laws.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand powers of products, combine factors and simplify a compound algebraic fraction.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts combine the index laws listed on page 3 with the algebraic-fraction simplification demonstrated on page 5 and powers of products demonstrated on page 6.
questions.methodNote: Apply the power-of-a-product law to coefficients and variables, multiply powers of the same base, then divide coefficients and subtract indices.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand powers of products, combine factors and simplify a compound algebraic fraction.

classification.difficultyReason: Reverse the power-of-a-product rule to recover missing bases or indices, including a zero index.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c and e–i recover factors or indices in powers of algebraic products, directly matching power-of-product-quotient. Part d additionally assesses zero-index-algebraic.
questions.methodNote: Apply the power-of-a-product and power-of-a-power laws in reverse; use the zero-index rule for part d. Check each completion by expanding its power.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reverse the power-of-a-product rule to recover missing bases or indices, including a zero index.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the negative-index definition directly and evaluate a numerical power.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses numerical negative-integer indices; no algebraic simplification or reciprocal fractional base is required.
questions.methodNote: Use a^{-n}=1/a^n, then evaluate the denominator, as demonstrated in Example 10 on PDF page 10.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the negative-index definition directly and evaluate a numerical power.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise a prime-power denominator and express its reciprocal using a negative index.

questions.mappingNote: Every part assesses numerical negative-index notation after recognising a prime-power denominator; part k uses the prime denominator itself with exponent −1.
questions.methodNote: Express the denominator as a power of a prime, then use 1/a^n = a^{-n}. Page 2 demonstrates prime-power recognition; page 9 defines negative indices; page 10 Example 10 demonstrates reciprocal powers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise a prime-power denominator and express its reciprocal using a negative index.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the reciprocal rule to single powers, coefficients and simple quotients, evaluating numerical powers where possible.

questions.mappingNote: Page 9 defines a^{-n}=1/a^n and states the reciprocal identity in both directions, supporting a–h. Page 10 Example 10 evaluates reciprocal numerical powers, supporting i–k. Page 11 retains the index laws for all integer indices. Page 12 Example 14 converts algebraic negative powers and combines reciprocal factors, supporting i–l. The available reuse candidates contain different tasks and are not source-equivalent.
questions.methodNote: Use a negative power as the reciprocal of the corresponding positive power. A reciprocal negative power becomes a positive power. Evaluate numerical powers and combine factors as a single fraction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the reciprocal rule to single powers, coefficients and simple quotients, evaluating numerical powers where possible.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply reciprocal powers, convert one mixed number to an improper fraction, and add signed indices for products with equal bases.

questions.mappingNote: Page 10 Example 11 supplies the method for a–d, including mixed-number conversion for c. Page 11 Example 12 supplies the signed-index addition method for e–h. Page 9 defines negative indices, and page 12 continues their application. The offered reuse candidates have different complete tasks and are not source-equivalent.
questions.methodNote: Use the reciprocal to replace a negative fractional power with a positive power. Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions first. For products with the same base, add the indices, then evaluate; a negative resulting index gives a reciprocal.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply reciprocal powers, convert one mixed number to an improper fraction, and add signed indices for products with equal bases.

classification.difficultyReason: Subtract indices for equal numerical bases, then evaluate the resulting negative power.

questions.mappingNote: Page 11 states the quotient and negative-index laws and supplies Example 13; its continued solution on page 12 models precisely the single-power, reciprocal and exact-evaluation sequence required in every part. Pages 9–10 establish and demonstrate reciprocal interpretation.
questions.methodNote: Use the quotient law to subtract indices for equal bases, then write the negative power as a reciprocal and evaluate exactly.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Subtract indices for equal numerical bases, then evaluate the resulting negative power.

classification.difficultyReason: Directly rewrite reciprocal powers using negative indices while retaining numerical coefficients.

questions.mappingNote: Page 9 defines negative indices; page 10 explains reciprocals; page 11 restates the negative-index law for non-zero algebraic bases; page 12 Example 14 applies it to algebraic factors. Each of a–f directly reverses this reciprocal conversion without requiring additional index laws.
questions.methodNote: Use the negative-index definition in reverse: 1/x^n = x^{-n}. Retain the numerical coefficient, including fractional coefficients.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Directly rewrite reciprocal powers using negative indices while retaining numerical coefficients.

classification.difficultyReason: For the mixed-number parts, convert to an improper fraction, take its reciprocal for the negative index, and evaluate the resulting positive power.

questions.mappingNote: Page 9 defines negative indices. Page 10 explains reciprocals and Example 11 demonstrates negative powers of fractions and a mixed number, directly supporting all six parts. Pages 11–12 confirm the index laws remain valid for negative integer indices.
questions.methodNote: A negative index means take the reciprocal and then evaluate the corresponding positive power. Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions before taking the reciprocal.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: For the mixed-number parts, convert to an improper fraction, take its reciprocal for the negative index, and evaluate the resulting positive power.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine signed exponents in multivariable products and quotients, simplify coefficients and express results with positive indices.

questions.mappingNote: Page 12 Example 14 directly demonstrates simplifying algebraic products and quotients with positive-index answers; page 11 states the laws for all integer indices, and pages 9–10 establish reciprocals. Parts a–f use addition of exponents; g–p use subtraction, including subtraction of negative indices.
questions.methodNote: Use product and quotient laws with integer indices, simplify coefficients, then replace negative powers by reciprocals; use the zero-index rule for cancelled variables.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine signed exponents in multivariable products and quotients, simplify coefficients and express results with positive indices.

classification.difficultyReason: Reverse product, quotient and power laws with negative indices, then construct suitable bases and exponents.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–h reverse the product and quotient laws in the page 11 summary and Examples 12–13. Parts i–j reverse the power-of-a-power law. Parts k–r use the reciprocal method on pages 9–10 and Example 14c–d on page 12.
questions.methodNote: Add indices for products, subtract for quotients and multiply for powers of powers. A negative power takes the reciprocal; powers distribute over products and quotients.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reverse product, quotient and power laws with negative indices, then construct suitable bases and exponents.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose a common factor of the supplied exponents to construct a base and outer power, then form another representation by reciprocating the base and negating the outer exponent. Parts q and r supply the target expressions and the preceding completions scaffold these routine reversed index laws.

questions.mappingNote: The concluding task refers to question 9q–r immediately above it. The page 11 laws and page 12 Example 14c–d support both positive-power and reciprocal negative-power representations.
questions.methodNote: Multiply indices when raising a power to a power, distribute powers over products and quotients, and use a reciprocal to reverse the sign of a power.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Choose a common factor of the supplied exponents to construct a base and outer power, then form another representation by reciprocating the base and negating the outer exponent. Parts q and r supply the target expressions and the preceding completions scaffold these routine reversed index laws.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand powers across products and quotients, handle division by negative powers, collect each variable's indices, and express the result with positive indices.

questions.mappingNote: Question 10 combines the methods of Example 14 with products and quotients of algebraic fractions. Applying index laws with negative integer indices is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Use the integer index laws, raise every factor in a product to the outside power, combine indices for common bases, and rewrite negative powers using reciprocals. Page 12 Example 14 demonstrates these algebraic methods.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand powers across products and quotients, handle division by negative powers, collect each variable's indices, and express the result with positive indices.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate exact integer roots using the inverse relationship between roots and powers; the final part also uses a power of a power.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–e directly evaluate integer roots using Example 15. Part f rewrites 2^10 as (2^2)^5 and takes the fifth root. Higher-order root evaluation is the primary assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 14 introduces roots as inverse powers. Page 15 defines nth roots and Example 15 evaluates roots by identifying the corresponding integer power or rewriting the radicand as a perfect power.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate exact integer roots using the inverse relationship between roots and powers; the final part also uses a power of a power.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert five roots to fractional indices and use a calculator to round each value to four decimal places.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d translate individual roots directly to reciprocal indices; part e also multiplies 7 by 1/3 to obtain the index 7/3. Conversion between surd and index notation is the common assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Use the definition a^{1/n}=the nth root of a, then evaluate with a calculator and round to four decimal places. Multiply indices for a power raised to a power, as demonstrated in the teaching.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert five roots to fractional indices and use a calculator to round each value to four decimal places.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise reciprocal indices as roots and evaluate familiar perfect powers.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve parts directly apply the reciprocal-index definition to perfect powers, matching Example 16.
questions.methodNote: Use a^{1/n} as the positive nth root of a. Example 16 evaluates reciprocal-index powers and verifies each result using the corresponding integer power.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise reciprocal indices as roots and evaluate familiar perfect powers.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate positive fractional powers by taking an integer root and then raising it to an integer power.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–h directly evaluate positive fractional indices; i–l express the same root-and-power relationship in radical notation. The printed margin reference is Example 17.
questions.methodNote: The positive fractional-indices definition and Example 17 on PDF page 16 evaluate the denominator root first, then the numerator power. Root and index notation are introduced on pages 14–15.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate positive fractional powers by taking an integer root and then raising it to an integer power.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply power, product and quotient laws to fractional indices, including common denominators and powers of coefficients.

questions.mappingNote: All sixteen parts assess fractional-index laws. Parts a–d use powers of powers; e–h products; i–l quotients; m–p also require powers of coefficients. Positive variables make the source's intended even-root simplifications valid.
questions.methodNote: Use the root definition of fractional indices and Example 18: multiply indices for a power of a power, add indices for products, subtract indices for quotients and form common denominators. Raise each factor of a product to the outside power.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply power, product and quotient laws to fractional indices, including common denominators and powers of coefficients.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine reciprocals with exact square, cube, fourth and fifth roots, including fractional bases.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses exact numerical evaluation of a negative fractional index; fractional-indices is the closest and most advanced directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Use the negative fractional-index definition and Example 19: take the reciprocal, then evaluate the positive fractional power using roots; fractional bases may be inverted first.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine reciprocals with exact square, cube, fourth and fifth roots, including fractional bases.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine fractional and negative indices using product, quotient and power laws, including numerical coefficients.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d use powers of powers and coefficients; e–h use addition of fractional indices; i–l use subtraction of negative fractional indices; m–o combine powers of products with reciprocal notation. All directly assess fractional indices.
questions.methodNote: Use fractional powers as roots, multiply indices for powers of powers, add or subtract indices for products or quotients, and rewrite negative powers as reciprocals. Example 20 begins on page 17 and its complete working continues on page 18.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine fractional and negative indices using product, quotient and power laws, including numerical coefficients.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise whole-number powers of ten by counting zeros.

questions.mappingNote: Every part reverses evaluation of a whole-number power of ten. The closest directly assessed catalogue skill is evaluate-index-notation; scientific notation coefficients are not requested.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 defines a positive integer power as repeated equal factors. Page 20 Example 21 explicitly identifies 100, 10 000 and 1 000 000 as powers of ten; pages 19–21 explain decimal movement and powers of ten.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise whole-number powers of ten by counting zeros.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise reciprocal powers of ten, including millionth and trillionth.

questions.mappingNote: Each part rewrites a reciprocal decimal power as a negative power of ten; no scientific-notation calculation is required.
questions.methodNote: Use the reciprocal-power definition a^{-n}=1/a^n. Page 21 explicitly identifies 10^6 as a million and 10^12 as a trillion.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise reciprocal powers of ten, including millionth and trillionth.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct conversion of large and small positive numbers into scientific notation.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses decimal-to-scientific-notation conversion. Negative-index definitions on pages 9–10 support the small-number conversions; pages 19–21 establish the scientific-notation convention.
questions.methodNote: Use a coefficient from 1 inclusive to 10 exclusive and multiply by the appropriate power of 10. Example 21 on PDF page 20 first expresses large numbers as a coefficient times a decimal power of ten; small numbers are expressed using division and reciprocal powers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct conversion of large and small positive numbers into scientific notation.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct conversion from scientific notation to decimal form using positive, zero and negative powers of ten.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve parts directly reverse scientific notation into ordinary decimal form; scientific-notation is the closest directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 22 on PDF page 20 expands positive powers of ten as whole-number multipliers and negative powers as reciprocal powers, then division, before evaluating. The zero-index definition supplies the multiplier 1 in part e.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct conversion from scientific notation to decimal form using positive, zero and negative powers of ten.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert a supplied large whole number directly into scientific notation.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses conversion of a large decimal numeral to scientific notation; no calculation with scientific notation is required.
questions.methodNote: Place the decimal point after the first non-zero digit and multiply by the corresponding power of 10, following Example 21 and the scientific-notation summary.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert a supplied large whole number directly into scientific notation.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert one positive whole-number rate into scientific notation.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses conversion to scientific notation; no speed calculation or unit conversion is required.
questions.methodNote: Place the decimal point after the first non-zero digit, then multiply by the appropriate power of ten, as demonstrated in Example 21.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert one positive whole-number rate into scientific notation.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct conversion of a small decimal to scientific notation, retaining kilograms.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses converting a small positive decimal to scientific notation; no calculation with two scientific-notation quantities is required.
questions.methodNote: Write the coefficient between 1 and 10, express division by 1000 as multiplication by its reciprocal, then use a negative power of 10, following Example 21e.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct conversion of a small decimal to scientific notation, retaining kilograms.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert a small positive decimal into scientific notation using a negative power of 10.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses conversion of a small decimal measurement to scientific notation, with its metre unit retained.
questions.methodNote: Example 21 on PDF page 20 converts small decimals by dividing the leading coefficient by a power of 10, writing the reciprocal, then using a negative index. Pages 19 and 21 define scientific notation with a coefficient from 1 inclusive to 10 exclusive; pages 9–10 establish reciprocal negative powers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert a small positive decimal into scientific notation using a negative power of 10.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply product, quotient and power laws, then normalise coefficients; later parts combine these operations.

questions.mappingNote: All sixteen parts assess calculations with scientific notation; parts k–p combine operations. None of the supplied reuse candidates is the same original task.
questions.methodNote: Use the reciprocal definition for negative indices, combine coefficients separately from powers of ten, apply product, quotient and power laws, then normalise to a coefficient between 1 and 10 as demonstrated in Example 23.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply product, quotient and power laws, then normalise coefficients; later parts combine these operations.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the supplied light-year definition to convert years into seconds, multiply by the speed of light and the number of light years, then normalise and round scientific notation.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed calculation multiplies scientific-notation quantities in a distance context. Speed–distance–time and time conversion are prerequisite methods whose explicit teaching is absent from the supplied pages.
questions.methodNote: Pages 19–20 define scientific notation and conversion; Example 23 on page 21 multiplies coefficients and combines powers of ten before normalising the coefficient. Pages 9–10 establish reciprocal powers. The solution uses the ordinary school convention of 365 days per year.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use the supplied light-year definition to convert years into seconds, multiply by the speed of light and the number of light years, then normalise and round scientific notation.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret a mass comparison as division, apply index laws and round the resulting count.

questions.mappingNote: The question assesses calculating a quotient of scientific-notation masses and interpreting the quotient as a count, matching calculations-scientific-notation.
questions.methodNote: Example 23(b) separates the coefficient quotient from the powers of ten and applies the quotient index law. Earlier negative-index definitions support subtracting negative exponents. Keep exact arithmetic until the requested whole-number rounding.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret a mass comparison as division, apply index laws and round the resulting count.

classification.difficultyReason: Select distance divided by speed, divide quantities in scientific notation and convert seconds to minutes.

questions.mappingNote: Scientific-notation division is directly taught. The speed–distance–time relationship and time conversion are prerequisite methods without explicit teaching in the supplied context.
questions.methodNote: Example 23(b), PDF page 21, divides coefficients and subtracts powers of ten. Apply this division to distance divided by speed, then divide seconds by 60 to obtain minutes.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select distance divided by speed, divide quantities in scientific notation and convert seconds to minutes.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert light years to kilometres using time-unit conversion and multiplication in scientific notation.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed chapter skill is calculation with scientific notation. Time conversion and the distance–speed relationship are prerequisites; their teaching is not supplied in the inspected chapter pages.
questions.methodNote: Pages 19–20 define scientific notation and conversion using powers of ten. Example 23 on page 21 multiplies coefficients and combines powers of ten, then normalises the coefficient. Apply that method after converting the light-travel duration to seconds; use distance = speed × time.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert light years to kilometres using time-unit conversion and multiplication in scientific notation.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate a large numerical expression, interpret one minute per outcome and convert the resulting duration into days and hours.

questions.mappingNote: The final assessed operation is duration conversion. The supplied scientific-notation teaching does not explicitly teach the prerequisite time conversions.
questions.methodNote: Pages 19–21 define scientific notation, demonstrate conversion and operations with powers of ten, and permit calculator use. Evaluate the supplied outcome count, then apply the given rate and convert minutes to hours and days.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate a large numerical expression, interpret one minute per outcome and convert the resulting duration into days and hours.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct application of scientific notation and rounding to three significant figures.

questions.mappingNote: Example 24 directly models the requested two-step process; Examples 21–22 establish scientific notation and the summary explains significant-figure rounding.
questions.methodNote: Write the number as a coefficient between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of 10, then round the coefficient to three significant figures, retaining significant trailing zeros.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct application of scientific notation and rounding to three significant figures.
